segments.text: Hello, hello, okay, the mic is on, great.
I am Hannah, I work on platform tooling, and I want to take some of the magic out of auto-instrumentation.
Raise your hand if you have turned on auto-instrumentation and then wondered what it is actually doing.
Yeah, that is most of the room, and that was me for about two years.
Let us start with what OpenTelemetry is, in one sentence.
It is a shared format and a set of libraries for traces, metrics, and logs, so every vendor speaks the same language.
A trace is the story of one request, broken into spans, where each span is one step with a start and an end.
Auto-instrumentation is a way to get those spans without writing tracing code in your app.
So how does it do that, and the answer depends a lot on the language.
In Java, there is an agent that rewrites classes as they load and wraps known libraries.
In Node, it hooks into module loading, so when your app requires the HTTP module, it gets a wrapped version back.
In Python, it patches functions at import time in a fairly similar way.
In every case, the trick is the same: it knows popular libraries and wraps their important functions.
So when your app makes a database query, the wrapped driver starts a span, runs the query, and ends the span.
It also passes a trace ID along in headers, so the next service can continue the same story.
That header passing is called context propagation, and it is the part that makes distributed tracing work.
Now in Kubernetes, there is one more layer, which is how the agent gets into your container at all.
An operator watches for new pods and changes them as they are created.
It adds an init container that copies the instrumentation files into a shared volume.
Then it sets a few environment variables, so the runtime loads those files when your app starts.
Your image does not change, your code does not change, the pod just starts with extra stuff attached.
That is why the pod needs to restart once after you turn it on, the changes only happen at creation.
Okay, so what do you get for free, and what do you not get.
You get spans for incoming HTTP requests, outgoing HTTP calls, and most popular database drivers.
You get timing, status codes, and the route that was matched.
You usually get logs connected to the trace, if your logger is one it knows.
What you do not get is anything about your business logic.
It does not know that this function is the checkout step or that this loop is processing an order.
For that, you add a few manual spans yourself, and that is fine, they mix with the automatic ones.
The other thing you do not get is free performance, there is a small cost to all this wrapping.
In our tests it was a few percent of CPU, which was fine for us, but measure it for yourself.
Sampling also matters a lot, and the defaults are not always what you want.
If you keep every trace from a busy service, your bill and your storage will both tell you about it.
We keep all errors and a small percentage of normal requests, and that has been enough to debug almost anything.
One more gotcha, if you already added an OpenTelemetry SDK by hand, do not also turn on the operator.
You end up with two sets of instrumentation fighting, and duplicated spans that are very confusing.
Pick one approach per service, and write down which one you picked.
Let me show the trace from our demo app, this is one request to the search page.
You can see the incoming request, then the database query, then the call out to the search service.
Nobody on the team wrote a single line of tracing code for this, and that still makes me happy.
So, wrap up: it wraps known libraries, it propagates context in headers, and the operator injects it at pod creation.
Thanks for listening, and I would love some questions.
Yes, you in the front.
So, um, what happens to the traces if the node running the collector dies?
Okay, so the question is what happens to traces when a node with the collector goes away.
Spans that were still in memory on that node are lost, there is no magic there.
Run the collector on more than one node, and the apps on other nodes keep sending traces to the copies that are still alive.
Over here.
Does auto-instrumentation slow down cold starts?
A little, yes, loading the extra files adds some startup time, in Node it was under a second for us.
If you run something where cold start really matters, like serverless functions, measure it before you commit.
Hi, can I turn it off for one service without touching the others?
Yes, the operator looks at annotations and namespaces, so you can leave one deployment out.
In our setup we only enable it for one namespace on purpose, so it leaves other teams' work alone.
Next.
How much does all this data cost to keep?
So, yeah, the honest answer is it depends on sampling more than anything else.
Keeping all errors and a small slice of normal traffic kept our bill boring, which is what you want.
Okay, I think we are out of time, thank you so much.
